stem: Ahmed is 7 years old and has exercise-induced asthma. He only gets symptoms when playing at school or playing soccer at the weekend. During your review, Ahmed mentions that his father drives him to soccer on the weekends and often smokes in the car. Ahmed’s mother does not smoke. What should be your response to this information?

options.text: Ignore it, Ahmed only reports exercise-induced symptoms
Suggest that Ahmed never get in the car with his father
Tell Ahmed’s father that he should not smoke in the car when his children are there
Ask the father if he has considered cutting down or quitting and discuss the benefits for Ahmed of reduced exposure to cigarette smoke

explanation: The best response is a brief, supportive discussion that encourages smoking reduction or cessation and explains the benefits of reducing Ahmed’s exposure to tobacco smoke. This is a family-centred, non-confrontational approach to addressing second-hand smoke exposure in a child with asthma.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Asthma Management: Medications and Devices - Part A

rationale: Second-hand smoke can worsen asthma symptoms and control. A supportive conversation about cutting down or quitting is usually the most appropriate initial response.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because second-hand smoke is relevant to asthma control and should not be ignored.
optionExplanations.B: Too extreme and impractical; it does not address smoking cessation or support behaviour change.
optionExplanations.C: This is appropriate advice, but it is more directive than the best first response in a consultation where supportive counselling is preferred.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. This is a collaborative, patient-centred way to address exposure and encourage smoking cessation/reduction.
